title: Feel the Emotion and Choose Your Response
learningGoals: Choose an action without obeying every impulse

deeperExplanation.question: How long should I stay with the sensation?
deeperExplanation.answer: Long enough to notice something useful can be brief. This is not an endurance exercise. You can notice a warm face or tight stomach, recognise the accompanying story, then orient outward and choose an action. If inward attention makes you more distressed or disconnected, return to the room, move or pause. The aim is a usable relationship with experience, not maximum intensity or a perfectly completed emotional process.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Feel the Emotion and Choose Your Response. Before speaking, you notice a tight stomach and a wish to avoid the moment. You tell yourself you must feel positive first, then become frustrated because the fear has not gone.

In this session, we will notice sensation, story and impulse, allow more than one feeling, and choose an action without obeying every impulse. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: An emotion can be acknowledged without being replaced immediately. Begin with what you notice: warmth, pressure, heaviness, restlessness or an urge to move. You may name the emotion if the name helps, but you do not have to identify it perfectly. Then notice the story that may be arriving with it. A sensation, a story and an action are related, but they are not the same thing.

sections.narration:
Before speaking, you notice a tight stomach and a wish to avoid the moment. You tell yourself you must feel positive first, then become frustrated because the fear has not gone.

Two experiences can coexist. You can feel afraid and want to speak. You can feel disappointed and still be interested in the next question. Choosing a constructive action does not require winning an argument against the feeling. You are making room for your experience while also keeping your purpose available.

If inward attention makes you more distressed or disconnected, return to the room, move or pause. The aim is a usable relationship with experience, not maximum intensity or a perfectly completed emotional process.

sections.narration: Imagine carrying a bag while walking somewhere important. You can notice its weight and adjust how you carry it. You do not always need to put it down before taking another step.

sections.narration: Orient to the room first. Use a mild recent feeling and notice one bodily feature for a few breaths without trying to change it. Then look outward again. Write the sensation, any accompanying story and one small action you would choose. If inward attention intensifies discomfort, use the room and the fictional example instead.

sections.narration: Let us try a small speaking experience. Give a short message on a mild everyday topic. Afterwards notice one sensation or feeling if it is available. A shorter attempt is fine. Record only when you choose. Afterwards save one observation rather than decide what this says about you as a person.

sections.narration: For this next attempt, keep one clear purpose. Continue the message with the feeling allowed to be present. If body attention is unhelpful, orient to the room and the meaning instead. No requirement to find an emotion. You can listen back if useful, or reflect without replaying. Changed, unchanged or uncertain experiences are all information.

sections.narration: Feeling a sensation is not a guaranteed way to make it disappear or discover its original cause. You can notice briefly and return to life. Strong feelings also permit a break or support. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Use sensation, story, choice once during a manageable moment. Keep the observation brief and choose a small constructive action. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.

sections.narration: Before leaving, save one observation in your own words. What would you keep, change or leave open? You can repeat this session, practise in another setting or choose a different tool. Your next step can be small. Return to your real situation with the part that feels useful today.
